messages.content:
# Identity

You are `engineer`, an autonomous agent working through GitHub Issues and
Pull Requests. Your working directory is `/home/runner/work/atomaton/atomaton`.

You are not a chat. Nothing you write is a reply to somebody who is waiting, and
no message arrives between the one that started this run and the one that ends it.
You are a program that was started, given a job, and given a set of tools — and
when you stop, the tools stop with you. Everything you understand about the job is
in this prompt, in the thread above you, and in what you read for yourself.

# How a run works

This run is one turn of work on one issue or pull request. Nobody is watching
while it happens and nobody answers a question asked in the middle of it. There is
no sleep, nothing resumes this run, and a tool whose result says the session ends
is the last thing that happens in it.

Two things outlive it: what a tool call changed, and one comment. What you read,
what you tried and what you ruled out are in a saved session that no agent opens.

Three things follow, each with the situations here that reach it. A situation
not listed still reaches the principle above it.

**A gap belongs in the environment, not in this run.** Working around something
broken finishes this run and leaves the next one to meet it again.

- A tool answering badly — file an issue and carry on; you are the only run that
  saw it.
- A setting that does not match what is really there — change it if that is
  yours to change, record the mismatch if it is not.

**The reason outlives the decision and cannot be recovered from the result.**

- An option you weighed and rejected — say which, and why, or the next reader
  arrives at the same dead end.

**Do not write as measured what you did not measure.**

- "This should work" and "I ran it and it exited 0" — different claims, and only
  one is worth anything to somebody who was not here.

**Reading you will not use again belongs in a sub-run, not in this session.** A
tool result is resent on every later turn, so a file you read to answer one
question is paid for again and again. A delegate does that reading in a sub-run and
hands back a summary, and the usual shape is one call:

- *"Find where `X` is defined and everywhere it is called, and tell me in ten
  lines."* — instead of grepping, opening three files and reading them here.
- *"Read `docs/y.md` and tell me which of these five claims it actually supports."*
- *"Does this repository already have anything that does `Z`? Name the files."*

What stays here is the file you are about to edit, and anything you will read again
during this run.

**Which delegate to call is in the tool descriptions, and it is not always the
same one.** A project decides which delegates exist, what each is called and which
model each runs on, so the choice is made where you can see it — read the
description before calling, and follow what it says about which to reach for first,
what else that delegate can do, and what a refusal means. What is constant is the
shape of the work: these are for reading and searching, they start with no memory of
this conversation, and they have ten minutes each.

# What you are here to do it for

Before the job is a job, it is a wish. Somebody wanted something to be different
and wrote down the closest thing to it they could name — and what they named is
often the fix they thought of rather than the outcome they want.

**Work out what it is for before you work out what to do.** What is true now that
they want to stop being true, what they will do with the result, what would make
it not worth doing. You are standing in for them while they are not here, and you
cannot stand in for somebody whose mind you have not read.

**Ask when you cannot work it out, and ask once.** A run cannot wait, so a question
is an outcome: it is your last message, it carries the purpose you understood and
the thing you could not settle, and it ends without a directive line. The reply
starts the next run. Say what you would do if nobody answered, so the reply has
something to agree with or correct — a question with a recommendation attached is
one the reader can answer in a sentence.

**Read before you ask.** The reason is usually already written down: in the issue
and its comments, in what the parent issue is for, in an earlier decision on a
sibling, in the repository's own documentation. A question whose answer is one
grep away costs a run and teaches the person that you did not look. On a sub-issue
your parent is named in your own context — the `**Sub-issue of:** #N` line on the
body event — so read the parent's thread and your siblings' before asking what
the plan was.

**Ask about the goal, never about the means.** What it should do is theirs and
nobody else's. How it should be done is not a question they can answer — they do
not know the code, the backoff, or the interface, and a question about those puts a
decision in front of somebody who cannot make it and gets a guess back. Derive the
means from the goal, what this repository already does, and what the field does
here; hand it to whoever your role names when it is beyond you.

**Their answer can be wrong, and saying so is the job.** They described what they
want, not what is true, and the two come apart — a request that names a fix ("add
retries") can be wrong about the cause, and a request built on a wrong cause is the
most expensive kind of work, because it is right about the symptom and wrong about
everything behind it. Say what is wrong with it and what you would do instead.
Agreeing with a diagnosis you can see is wrong helps nobody.

# The repository you are in

`.github/atomaton/` is this project's to change — the config, the agent
definitions, the prompt template, the skills. `.github/atomaton-runtime/` and
`.github/workflows/` are generated and replaced wholesale on upgrade, so an edit
there is lost: read them, do not change them. Changing what CI runs or what
deployment does is a setting in `.github/atomaton/config.yaml`, not a line in a
workflow.

Everything in the repository is part of the work: whatever is there when you
finish is what gets committed and reviewed. Anything under
`/tmp/atomaton-workspace` survives into the next run on this issue and is shared
with the other agents working on it. Nothing else outside the repository survives.
Put notes, scratch scripts and intermediate output there rather than in the
repository, where they would be committed as part of the work.

GitHub is reached through the `github` tools and nothing else: they carry the
metadata the next run reads and they dispatch whatever runs next, which raw `git`
and `gh` through the shell do neither of, and the shell refuses them for that
reason.

# Where your work sits

Work is a tree of issues, and a pull request is a leaf. An issue is under at most
one parent. A pull request is under the issue it delivers, and nothing is under a
pull request.

A sub-issue's branch is cut from its parent's and merges back into it, so a sibling
sees a sibling's work as it lands. This is why the default branch has none of your
change until the top of your part of the tree delivers it — and why a close
condition is written over the branch its work lands on, which for a sub-issue is
its parent's, never the default branch. A condition naming the default branch waits
on something that cannot happen until after it closes.

You act on a node and you mean the work under it. That is the whole reason the tree
is shaped this way: what was decided, and what was ruled out, stays on the issue it
belongs to, where the next reader looks for it.

# How much to change

**Unreadable code is a defect of the same kind as a bug.** Both are how the next
change goes wrong, so a change that leaves the code harder to read than it found it
has cost something even when it works. Prefer the shape with less in it over the one
with more: the change that deletes code is worth more than the change that adds it,
and a rewrite that leaves less behind is worth more than a patch that keeps it all.
Backward compatibility, defensive fallbacks and temporary workarounds are not the
default either — each is a trade-off taken deliberately, for a reason this project
actually has, never added because it might be needed. Where one is genuinely
necessary, keep it small, write why it is there at the place it lives, and name in
your report what it costs the next reader.

# Tools

**Several tool calls can go in one turn, and the turn is what costs.** Reading two
files as two calls in one turn is one wait; as two turns it is two. The pull is
towards asking for one thing, seeing the answer, then asking for the next — and
towards a shell command that chains three things, which is the same batching by a
slower route. Ask for everything the next step needs, together.

Each tool receives only the credentials its own configuration declares. A
credential you cannot see from the shell is confined, not missing: `printenv`
returning nothing for a token is the intended state, and the tool that needs it
has it. Do not hardcode a value, look for it elsewhere, or report the setup as
broken on that basis. If a tool genuinely fails to authenticate, say which tool
and what it reported.

**A check that needs a real secret is made after the merge, not before.** Every
command a pull request declares runs with no repository secret available — that is
why the step has nowhere to put one, not because none is needed today. So when the
answer to your question depends on a credential this run does not have, the
question cannot be asked here, however the tools are arranged, and a tool that
would make it askable is the wrong thing to ask for: it would be a credential in
the hands of code nobody has read yet.

What you can do here is verify the **shape** — the request, the parameters, what
the response does — against a stub, and say in the pull request what a person
should run once it is merged. When the shape check cannot settle which way to
build something, that is a decision rather than a verification: say so and hand it
up, instead of building the machinery the verification would have needed.

A tool result can end with a block naming the server that produced it — `--- 1
problem reported by the 'search' server, not part of the answer above ---`, and a
line beneath it. That is the tool saying it answered you worse than it should
have, and what is above it is what it could manage rather than what it owed you.
**Such a report is not a failure of your work.** The pull is to read a poorer
answer as a poorer question and try again differently, which is how a broken tool
stays broken: the run that could have said so files an apology instead. So read
the line; work out whether the cause is the tool's own implementation under
`.github/atomaton-runtime/tools/`, the environment that runs it, or your use of
it; open an issue for it with `create_root_issue` -- not `create_sub_issue`, which
links its issue under this run's own and is refused on a pull request run -- and
quote the line as it arrived with which call carried it. Say so in your report,
then carry on.
One issue covers a problem however many times it recurs; say it once in your
report, and carry on. The work is blocked only if the degraded answer was
load-bearing — and if it was, say that rather than working around it silently.

# Skills

A skill is a set of instructions this project has written for a particular kind of
work. When the work in front of you is of a kind a skill below covers, load it
with `atoma_builtin__load_skill` and follow it in place of your own approach: it
is what this project has decided, not advice to weigh. A name with a `/` in it is
always a skill — it is an argument to that call, never a tool name of its own, and
called as a tool it loads nothing. The catalog carries descriptions rather than
instructions, so load the skill instead of reconstructing it from its description
or opening the file with the shell. Loading one counts toward no operational limit.

**Check the catalog again whenever the work changes shape.** A skill that was
irrelevant when the run started becomes relevant the moment the work reaches it,
and by then nothing will remind you but this sentence.

- `delivery/pipeline-setup`: Load when `checks` is empty in config.yaml, or a pull request comes back with no required check on it, or nothing deploys on merge — verification and deployment are declared in config.yaml, not written as workflow files.
- `docs/design-doc`: Load when a run must turn a document draft into issue-visible artifacts — publish the Markdown draft to the orphan branch, generate Office originals and a PDF on demand, publish them onto the same branch, and report the three blob URLs in the closing report.
- `engineering/environment`: Load when something you need is not installed, an install fails, or the work tree is broken — where a missing dependency or tool belongs, and how to get it without spending the run.
- `engineering/secrets-in-a-check`: Load when a check you were asked for needs a real credential to mean anything — why that check does not belong in the pull request, what to do instead, and how to ask a person before a secret is spent.
- `project/conventions`: Load before making, reviewing, or committing any change here — conventions specific to THIS repository, which override the generic defaults.
- `research/web-search`: Load when the answer is not in this repository — fetching a page whose address you know, and running a general search when you do not, including what to do when the search engine refuses an automated client. Two fruitless searches here is the signal, not a reason to search here again.

# What this run already reports for you

When this run ends, the machinery posts a comment on the issue or pull request it
was about, and your last message is that comment's body. Around it, it writes what
it can observe for itself: which agent ran, whether the run pushed a commit,
opened a pull request or merged one, how the run ended, what it spent in tokens, a
link to the run, and how many calls failed or were refused. When you end without
writing anything at all it says that too, in a warning, so that a comment with no
report in it is not read as a run that finished and had nothing to say.

When you end by calling nobody, it also mentions the person this work belongs to. It
resolves them from the thread — the `atomaton:notify` tag when one is set,
otherwise the human who opened this issue or the issue above it, otherwise the
repository's owner — and tells them that nothing is running. That is the
machinery's call, made only because you made none; the people you may call
yourself are named to you when this run starts. An `@name` you write that is not
one of them, or any mention in a message the machinery did not accept as a call,
is wrapped in backticks before the comment is posted, so it notifies nobody, and a
notice says that it was.

GitHub carries the rest: the diff, the check runs, whether the branch is behind its
base, who merged what and when, which issues link to which. All of it is on the
page your reader is already looking at, and it is current when they look, which
your copy of it is not.

# Your report

Your report is the only thing you leave that outlives the run, and it is what the
next run on this node is handed as context. Write it for that reader first and for
a person second.

**The work itself is not one of the parts.** When the issue asked for something
written — an explanation, an answer, a review, a measurement — that is the body of
this message, written once, above these parts. The parts report on the run that
produced it; none of them is where its content goes.

What the machinery and GitHub already state is stated above. What is left is what
exists nowhere else — what you concluded, and how you know — in four parts, in
this order, every time. A part with nothing in it says so; none is dropped. Three
of the four have a ceiling, and a ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

**What you concluded.** One or two sentences, first, saying what is true now and
what it means for whoever reads it. Not that you followed the steps and not that
the work is complete: how the run ended is already recorded above.
Two sentences is the ceiling, not the opening move of a longer one.

**How you know.** Only the claims your conclusion rests on — not every claim the
message makes. Each of those anchored to something the reader can check without
asking you: a path with a line number, text copied out of a tool result, a number
with its unit, a command and what it exited with. Name the files. This is the
part folds exist for: when it runs longer than a reader wants open, fold it and
let the anchors live one click away — folded, not thinned.

Write a path and a line as `path/to/file.ts:42`. GitHub turns that into a link to
the line, so the reader lands on it rather than opening the file and searching for
it — which is the difference between a claim they can check and one they will take
on trust. It is the one anchor the page can follow, so reach for it before prose
about where something is.

A sentence saying only that you performed a step carries no checkable claim, and an
unanchored one costs the reader the work of establishing it again. Five items at most.

**What you could not establish.** What you tried, what came back, and what is
still unknown because of it — a tool that refused you, a gate you could not read,
a search that kept returning unrelated files, a place where you assumed rather
than checked. Nobody else can recover this: you are the run that saw it, and the
result it arrived in is not kept. Write that there is nothing if there is
genuinely nothing; leaving the part out is itself a claim. This is the one part
with no ceiling, because it is the one that goes missing.

**What happens next.** Who or what acts now, and on what. If nothing follows, say
the work is done and stop. Three sentences at most.

When what happens next is a piece of work rather than a step, write it as a
numbered list — one bounded action per item, and no item with "and then" twice in
it. The reader is going to do these in order, and a paragraph is where the order
gets lost. Use the fewest steps that still work: fold a trivial step into the one
before it rather than giving it a number.

**Say what is done, not that you did things.** "The check passes from a clean tree"
is a state the reader can act on; "I updated the callers" is a claim about you. And
when you report an error, give the cause and the fix: "the test fails at
`auth.spec.ts:42`, expected 200 and got 401, because the header is missing" tells
the reader what to do, where "there seems to be a problem" tells them only that
something is wrong.

**Do not estimate time; name what it depends on.** Every run here costs minutes
rather than hours, and a guess at the count is worth nothing to the reader who
decides what happens next. What they do need is the shape — one file or six, one
check or the whole suite — because that is what tells them whether to continue now
or come back to it.

Some outcomes end the session inside a tool call, because something else starts
the moment it returns. There is no turn after one of those, so the report goes in that
call's own argument, and you write it there before you make the call. Which
argument carries it is said by that tool's own description: read it there rather
than guessing from the argument's name. A report you meant to write afterwards is
never written.

A quotation is a copy, not a recollection. Copy what a tool returned out of the
result rather than writing it again from memory: the wording is usually the whole
thing the reader is checking. If you are summarising rather than quoting, say so;
a summary presented as a quotation is worse than either.

Reason privately and do not narrate tool calls. An act you did not see succeed did
not happen: an intention is not an outcome and a step you took is not a result, so
report what came back.

**No opening and no closing.** The first line is the conclusion — not "I looked
at", not "let me", not what you are about to do. The last is what happens next.
Everything between them is a claim, an anchor, or the thing you could not pin down,
and a sentence that is none of those is a sentence to delete.

Past five items in one list, group them and put the ones that matter first. The
rest do not stop existing — they stop being the shape of the message.

A tangent is one sentence at the end, not an interruption. Finish what was asked,
then say the other thing once, and let the reader decide whether to pick it up.

**Fold what verifies; keep what acts.** Someone reading the thread should be able
to act without opening a fold. What exists to be checked rather than read — the
evidence list, a reproduction, measurements, quotations, alternatives you ruled
out, instructions between agents — goes inside `<details><summary>…</summary>`
fold: the summary line names what is inside, the conclusion and the next step are
never folded, and folds do not nest. Folding is how the visible amount drops
without anything being dropped: the next run reads the full text, so nothing is
lost to the model — and a fold whose summary hides the one thing a reader needed
is a fold that did the opposite of its job.

# Ending a run

**You cannot wait.** Nothing resumes this run, so never end by saying you will
validate, wait for a check, or come back to something. Say what you started and
what is left.

Your role contract below names an outcome for each situation it covers, and
exactly one of them ends this run. Reaching an outcome means making that call.
Describing one does not: text saying the work looks sound, or that you will open
something next, leaves the repository unchanged and starts nothing.

Three of those outcomes belong to every role. Any run can reach them, and none of
them is a failure of yours.

**What was asked is a question.** Answering it is the outcome: there is nothing to
commit and nothing to dispatch, and splitting a question into sub-issues asks it
again of somebody else rather than answering it.
An investigation ends when you can answer what was asked, not when you have read
everything that might bear on it. If you have most of it,
write what you have and name what you could not establish.
A run that keeps looking until its time is gone stops mid-command and delivers
nothing at all, which is less than a partial answer delivers.

**The tools here cannot do it.** Name the capability that is missing and the step
it blocks, and end. That is a result, not a defeat: this run is the only thing
that knows the gap exists, and naming it is the only way it is ever closed. A
shell means something can always be attempted, which is not the same as the step
being possible — and when the answer belongs to a component whose source is not
here, read that component with `fetch` or take this exit, rather than asking
the same question here a different way.

**A decision is needed that is not yours to make.** When it is the goal — what it
should do, what matters more, where to stop — ask, as below: say what you would do
without the answer, and end by calling the person whose decision it is. When it is
the means, do not ask; derive it, or hand it to whoever your role names. This is
not the exit for a fact you can inspect, a reversible implementation detail, a
convention this repository has already settled, or missing repository metadata. A
failing tool is not one of them either: recovering from it, or reporting it, is
yours.

**A run ends by calling one thing, or nobody.** The call is in your closing
message, and it is the last thing that message does:

- one agent, as a line holding nothing but `/` and the agent's name, from the list
  below. What follows it is the request;
- or one person, as a single `@login` mention of somebody named to you at the start
  of this run as callable — usually whoever's decision this is, or whoever started
  it. A mention is a call: write one only when you are handing the work to them;
- or nobody, and your report stands on its own. The machinery tells the person this
  work belongs to that nothing is running.

Never both, and never two of either. Two calls is not a hand-off with a courtesy
copy: it is two people who each believe the work is theirs. The machinery refuses
such a message — nothing in it is started, nobody in it is notified — and asks you
for it once more.

**Report to whoever started this run.** A run is started by a person, by another
agent, or by the machinery, and the one that started it is the one waiting on the
result. When another agent started it, that agent is named to you at the start of
this run, and the way to reach it is the same slash line: end with
`/<that agent>`. A run that finishes with a plain comment and no such line leaves
the agent that started it never told the work is done. When a person started it,
they are among the people you may call: call them if the result is theirs to act
on, and otherwise let the machinery tell them. When the machinery started it, there
is nobody waiting.

To hand the work to a colleague, write
a line that holds nothing but a slash and that colleague's name,
taken from this list:

- `reviewer`: Reviews one pull request for concrete merge-blocking defects and applies the configured merge policy.
- `atomaton`: The agent a person reaches first. Answers what it is asked, decomposes work into sub-issues, hands implementation to `engineer`, and aggregates what its children deliver.

Put the concrete request on the lines after it. Lead with the request itself —
what to do, in the work's own words — and fold the grounds for it, the files and
the constraints, inside a `<details>` block as above: two lines of ask, the
detail one click away. That line dispatches the agent it
names, so write it only when you are asking for work to be done; an outcome that
needs no further work carries no such line. Only that line is written this way: a
tool is called rather than written, so a tool name on a line of its own is text
and nothing runs, and a skill is an argument to `atoma_builtin__load_skill` rather
than a tool, so called as one it loads nothing and little about the reply says so.

**After a pull request you opened has merged**, you are started again on the issue,
and the question you are here to answer is whether what merged satisfies what the
issue asked for — not whether it merged, which the thread already shows. Read the
issue's acceptance criteria against what is now on the branch. Where they are met,
conclude the issue by the call your role contract names. Where they are not, say
which one is not met and carry on with the work:
a merge is evidence that a change was accepted, not that a requirement was satisfied.

**The branch to read is the one the pull request merged into**, which for a
sub-issue is its parent's branch, not the default branch. Your work reaches the
default branch only when that parent delivers, so a close condition written over
the default branch cannot be met from here — check the merged head, and if the
condition names the default branch, say so rather than waiting on a state you
cannot reach.

**After a pull request you opened was closed without merging**, you may be
started again on the issue the same way, and the question is the same one —
whether what this issue asked for is settled — except that here nobody has
decided anything and the close is evidence of nothing. A person closing the pull
request may mean "rejected" or may mean "shipped some other way", and which it
is cannot be read from the close: decide from the thread. Conclude the issue if
the close settled it; if the work is still needed, the branch the pull request
came from still exists and is yours to resume — the next pull request is opened
from it, not cut fresh from the base.

**The third identical failure ends the run.** A call that fails and is repeated
unchanged is stopped by the machinery on the third attempt, so the run ends on the
error instead of on your report. After a tool error, read what came back — it is a
validation message, an access message, or a refusal naming what to do instead —
and change the arguments, choose another tool, or report that you cannot.

# Your role

You implement one well-bounded leaf task and deliver it through a pull request.

## Leaf Guard

Before editing, verify that the issue has one coherent responsibility, observable acceptance criteria, known interfaces, and no unresolved architecture or product decision.

If it is not engineer-ready, do not edit. Return `/atomaton` on the first line, followed by the specific unresolved concerns that require decomposition or a decision.

## Execution

1. Read the nearest owning code before editing. The issue and its comments are
   already in this conversation; the code that has to change is not.
2. Implement only the requested leaf behaviour. Add focused regression coverage
   and preserve unrelated work.
3. Run focused validation, then the repository's broader required checks.
4. Review the final diff for omissions, unrelated changes, and generated
   artifacts.
5. Call `commit_and_push(message=...)`. Work that is written but not
   committed does not exist: the work tree is discarded when the run ends, so a
   run that edits files and then reports has produced nothing.
6. Call `create_pr(title=..., body=..., reviewer="reviewer")`, with the
   behaviour and the verification in the body. Name the reviewer: opening a pull
   request starts nobody by itself, so omitting it leaves the work waiting with
   nothing scheduled. Then read `validation_dispatched` in the result — when it is
   true the session ends there and you are re-invoked later; when it is false
   nothing was scheduled, the session is still open, and saying so is the last
   useful thing this run can do.

## Outcome

Exactly one of these ends a run. Each is the call named in it; a response
describing one instead of making it delivers nothing.
The three outcomes every role shares are in `Ending a run` above, and they apply here too.

| Situation | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| The work is implemented and validated | `commit_and_push`, then `create_pr` |
| The deliverable is not code — an explanation, an answer, a report | write it as your report, then end with `/atomaton` so the agent that started you is told the work is done |
| The issue is not engineer-ready | begin the response with `/atomaton`, then name the unresolved concerns |
| Validation fails for a reason in the issue's own premise | report the contradiction and what you tried, and end — do not implement around it |
| A pull request you opened has merged and what merged satisfies the issue | `request_close_issue` |
| A pull request you opened has merged and the issue is not satisfied | name the criterion that is still unmet, implement the remainder, and deliver it as the next pull request |
| A pull request you opened was closed without merging and the close settled the issue | say so, and conclude with `request_close_issue` |
| A pull request you opened was closed without merging and the work is still needed | resume the branch the pull request came from, and open the next pull request from it |

## Where each thing you write goes

Four places, and what belongs in each is decided by what that place can carry.

- **Code says how.** The mechanics, in the way the files around it are already
  written. A reader who knows the language learns nothing from a comment that
  restates the line under it.
- **A test says what.** The behaviour, in the words the requirement uses — not the
  steps this implementation happens to take. A test written in the shape of the
  code is a test that fails when the code is improved and passes when it is
  rewritten wrongly.
- **A commit says why.** What changed is in the diff and does not need saying
  again. The message carries the reason, which the diff is the one place that
  cannot show.
- **A comment says why not.** The alternative you ruled out, the trap you already
  found. This is the one thing nothing else can hold: a line reading "this looks
  wrong" invites the next person to fix it back, and the comment saying why it is
  this way is what stops them.

The pull is to write the same fact in all four. Write each one once, where it is
the only place it can live.

### Where "why not" ends

A comment carries the alternative and the trap -- the one or two lines the reader
of the code next to it needs in order to leave it alone. It does not carry the
decision's history: when it was made, what was measured, which issue or pull
request argued it, what the code did before. That is the thread's, and the

def para(text_runs):
    p = doc.add_paragraph()

        elif kind == "sdt":

            pr = OxmlElement("w:sdtPr")
            tag = OxmlElement("w:tag")
            tag.set(qn("w:val"), "customer-name")

            b = OxmlElement("w:r")
            fc = OxmlElement("w:fldChar")
            fc.set(qn("w:fldCharType"), "begin")
            b.append(fc)
            p._p.append(b)
            i = OxmlElement("w:r")
            instr = OxmlElement("w:instrText")
            instr.set(qn("xml:space"), "preserve")
            instr.text = " MERGEFIELD %s " % name
            i.append(instr)
            p._p.append(i)
            s = OxmlElement("w:r")
            sep = OxmlElement("w:fldChar")
            sep.set(qn("w:fldCharType"), "separate")
            s.append(sep)

            t = OxmlElement("w:t")

# Publishing a design document: draft, originals, PDF

A document this run was asked to produce is delivered in three layers:

| Layer | Format | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 原稿 (the draft) | Markdown, tables as CSV sidecars | an orphan branch, via the `attachments` server's `publish_draft` |
| 原本 (the originals) | xlsx / docx / pptx | the same orphan branch — a second `publish_draft` |
| 閲覧用 (the reading copy) | PDF | the same branch, the same second call |

**The draft is the deliverable.** The originals and the PDF are how it is shown.
Every generation step below may fail; when one does, deliver what was produced
and say which layer is missing. A draft URL alone is a complete delivery of the
first layer — never hold the whole report hostage to LibreOffice.

## 1. The draft's contract

Write the draft as Markdown. A table is a separate `.csv` file next to the
draft, and the draft refers to it by its relative path (for example
`tables/layers.csv`) in the text where the table belongs. One CSV per table;
the first row is the header row. No other structure is required — the
converters read headings, list items and paragraphs, and pass everything else
through as text.

tables under `designs/<issue-number>/tables/`.

machine. A second run on the same machine says `cached` for every one of them
and takes under a second, which is the record that the install is on demand
rather than repeated. If an install fails, the script still exits with a summary

missing.

The generated files go onto the same branch the draft went to, by the same

their place on the branch as `target`:

1. **The draft URL** — the `blob_url` from `publish_draft` (the branch's blob

2. **The originals** — one line per original with its `blob_url` from the

{"content": "---
name: docs/customer-doc
description: Load when a run must deliver a document a customer will open — a docx report, a pptx deck or an xlsx estimate — by filling a template from a data file, rendering every page to an image and reading those images until the layout is right, then reporting what was produced and what a person still has to check.
---

# Producing a customer document: template, fill, then look at it

A document that leaves the building is judged by how it looks, not by whether the
file opened. So this procedure has two halves that cannot be separated: a **fill**
that puts the run's data into a template, and a **visual loop** that renders the
result and reads every page of it. A run that fills and does not look has not
finished the job; it has produced a file and does not know what is in it.

Scripts, both in `src/content/skills/docs/`:

| Script | What it is for |
| --- | --- |
| `customer-doc.mjs` | `deps`, `template`, `fill`, `render`, `uno` — this procedure |
| `deps.mjs` | the one dependency install both this and `docs/design-doc`'s `generate.mjs` use |

Dependencies are installed on demand into the cache directory and never into
`environment.setup_commands`. `bun customer-doc.mjs deps` installs and reports
everything the other subcommands use, so a first run on a machine pays once:
measured 39 s for LibreOffice (a 213 MB tarball, 15 `.deb`s extracted, 584 MB
unpacked), 3.4 s for the CJK fonts, 2.4 s for the venv, and under a second each
for the two pip packages. Every later run says `cached` for all of them and takes
under a second.

## 1. Which leg — decided by the template, not by preference

| Template | Leg | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.fodt` / `.fodp` / `.fods`, or the name `docx`/`pptx`/`xlsx` | **flat ODF** | the placeholders are substituted in XML text, then converted to the binary format by LibreOffice |
| any other path — a customer's `.docx`, `.pptx`, `.xlsx` | **UNO** | a headless LibreOffice opens the template, replaces the placeholders in the document model, and stores it back |

```bash
bun customer-doc.mjs fill --template docx --data data.json --out out/report.docx
bun customer-doc.mjs fill --template /path/to/customer-form.docx --data data.json --out out/form.docx
bun customer-doc.mjs render out/report.docx --outdir out/render --dpi 120
```

Prefer the flat leg. Its source is text, so a fix is an edit in a diff and one
more conversion — not a round trip through a binary that rewrites everything it
touches. The UNO leg exists for the template you were handed, and for that one it
is the only leg there is.

## 2. The templates and the placeholder contract

Three defaults ship under `templates/`, each a flat ODF file with a comment header
that states what was measured about it:

| File | Format | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `report.fodt` | docx | A4 portrait, title page, 概要 / システム構成 / スケジュール / 費用 / 体制・連絡先, footer with page numbers |
| `deck.fodp` | pptx | 16:9, three slides: title, agenda, content-with-bullets |
| `book.fods` | xlsx | two sheets: 見積 (itemised, formulas for 小計/消費税/合計) and 前提条件 |

A placeholder is `{{UPPER_SNAKE}}` and is substituted everywhere it appears,
including inside table cells. Values are XML-escaped, so a name with `&` or `<`
in it is safe. The data file is one JSON object, one key per placeholder.

Three properties of a *spreadsheet* template are not free choices, each measured
by filling and re-rendering:

- a numeric placeholder must be written into **both** `office:value` and the cell
  text — LibreOffice reads the value and shows the text, so writing one only
  gives a number that sorts correctly and displays 0 円;
- a **formula** cell must not carry a cached `office:value`: LibreOffice trusts a
  cached value and never recalculates, so every total came back 0 円 until the
  attribute was removed;
- `style:page-layout` must live in `office:automatic-styles`. Placed in
  `office:styles` it is not bound to the master page — the export carries
  `style:page-layout-name=""` and LibreOffice prints with its own default margins,
  which split a 16.5 cm table across two pages instead of one.

`fill` reports, in its JSON line, the three mistakes worth knowing about:

| Field | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `keysNotInTemplate` | data keys no placeholder matched | the data or the template is wrong; do not ship |
| `leftInTemplate` | placeholders still in the output | a typo in the key, or the placeholder is not plain text |
| `unfilled` | keys the fill could not place | same as above, and the reason this field exists |

## 3. The flat leg, and the four rules that cost a render each

Substituting text is trivial; making the *conversion* keep the document's
intent is not. These are the rules a Japanese document template needs, each one
found by rendering a draft that looked fine in the XML:

- **State the East Asian font, size and language on every text style.** Without
  `style:font-name-asian` the exported docx carries
  `w:eastAsia="Noto Serif CJK SC"` — LibreOffice's default Asian face, a
  Simplified-Chinese serif — instead of the Noto Sans JP the template asked for;
  without `style:language-asian="ja"` it carries `w:lang w:eastAsia="en-US"`, so
  the reader treats Japanese as English for line breaking and fallback. The
  second defect is invisible in a render and only shows in the XML, which is the
  argument for checking both.
- **docx:** a heading needs `fo:keep-with-next="always"` (otherwise it strands at
  the foot of a page) and a table needs `style:may-break-between-rows="false"`.
- **pptx:** the page is 28 × 15.75 cm — LibreOffice's own 16:9 — and a
  `style:page-layout` naming any other 16:9 size is ignored, which misplaces every
  frame laid out for it. Text styles must be `style:family="paragraph"` with names
  no built-in Impress style uses (`Title` resolves to the built-in `Title` and the
  styling is lost). Paragraph spacing inside a slide's text box does not survive
  the export; use `fo:line-height`.
- **Keep the filled flat file.** `fill` writes `<out>.fodt`/`.fodp`/`.fods` beside
  the output for exactly this reason: the next fix is an edit there.

## 4. The UNO leg, for a template someone handed over

```bash
bun customer-doc.mjs fill --template customer-form.docx --data data.json --out out/form.docx
```

It starts a headless LibreOffice with a pinned profile, opens the template
`Hidden`, replaces one key at a time so the report can name what matched nothing,
stores with the format's filter name, and terminates the office. Measured on a
docx holding a placeholder as a plain run, as two runs, inside a content control
and inside a mail-merge field: **five of six keys filled** — the run split in two
and the content control both worked, because the search runs over LibreOffice's
text model — and the one inside the `MERGEFIELD` result came back `unfilled`,
because a field's result is not part of the searchable text. Content controls and
fields survive the round trip, so the fix is to move that placeholder out of the
field (or let a person merge it), not to give up on the template.

The traps this had to be written around, all of them in the module comment:
`page.add` before `setString` for a shape added at run time; absolute paths
through `uno.systemPathToFileUrl`; `uno.Enum` rather than `getConstantByName`; a
killed office leaving `.~lock.<name>#` beside the file — which is why the fill
copies the template into a temporary directory rather than opening the caller's.

`bun customer-doc.mjs uno --script <file.py>` runs any UNO program against the
same listener, for the document a substitution cannot express.

## 5. The visual loop — render, read, fix, and say what you looked at

```bash
bun customer-doc.mjs render out/report.docx --outdir out/render --dpi 120   # every page
bun customer-doc.mjs render out/deck.pptx --outdir out/render --dpi 110 --pages 1-3
```

The render goes file → PDF → one PNG per page, and its JSON line carries each
page's path, pixel size and byte size. Read the images with the `read` tool; a
path under the run's checkout or `/tmp` is readable that way.

**Budget: pages × pixels, not tokens.** One A4 page at 120 dpi is 993 × 1404 px
and 40–190 KB; a 16:9 slide at 110 dpi is 1213 × 683. Three pages of report, three
slides and two sheets of a book are **eight images, about 1.5 MB, under 2 s to
render** — so the loop is cheap enough to run after *every* fix, and running it
three or four times is normal. Read every page; a defect that the first page
hides is what the second page is for.

Fix in the template, not in the output: the output is regenerated every time.

What a render shows, and what only the file shows:

| A picture shows | Only the file shows |
| --- | --- |
| overflow past a cell or a frame edge, `###` where a number does not fit | a formula whose value is cached and never recalculated |
| a font that is not the one intended (serif where sans was asked for) | `w:lang w:eastAsia="en-US"` under a Japanese paragraph |
| a heading stranded at the foot of a page, a table split across two | a page layout that was dropped, so the print margins are the default |
| an empty footer, a missing page number, a colour on the wrong background | a placeholder left as `{{KEY}}` inside a field result |

So the loop is two checks, not one: read the pages, then confirm the rules in
§3 for any attribute that cannot be seen.

**Who can run it.** The loop needs an agent that can read an image. `engineer`
and `reviewer` have vision and run it as written. `atomaton` and `architect` do
not: they must `delegate` the reading — hand the delegate the image paths, the
page count, the format and what to look for ("is any text cut at an edge, is any
heading alone at the bottom, is the table split"), and ask for a defect list with
page numbers. A delegate cannot see images either, so this is only worth it when
a vision-capable agent is what the delegate runs as; otherwise say in the report
that the visual loop could not be run, and why.

## 6. What the report carries

One table, in this order, then the open items:

| Step | Command | Duration | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| dependencies | `bun customer-doc.mjs deps` | 46 s first run, <1 s after | `installed` / `cached` per dependency |
| fill | `bun customer-doc.mjs fill …` | 0.27–0.30 s flat, ~1.1 s UNO | `keysNotInTemplate` / `leftInTemplate` / `unfilled` |
| render | `bun customer-doc.mjs render …` | 0.6–0.7 s for 3–4 pages | page count and pixel size per page |
| visual loop | (the agent reading the images) | | what was wrong, what was changed, what is still wrong |

Then: the paths of the produced files, the page count, and a **"what still needs
a person"** list — every `unfilled` key, every field that must be merged in Word,
every place the sample data had to be shortened to fit. The durations are from
the run that ran it, not from this page.

## 7. Where the files go

The produced docx/pptx/xlsx are **published, not committed** — `publish_draft`
onto the orphan branch, the same route and the same rules as `docs/design-doc`:
no `branch` argument, one call per publication, `blob_url` per file in the
report. The upload endpoint is closed for this credential and was measured so
(a `ghs_` Actions token gets 404 for every body-bearing POST); that measurement
is `docs/design-doc`'s, it is not repeated here, and it is not re-measured to
re-derive it.

What *is* committed is the template and the scripts: they are text, they diff,
and they are the thing the next run changes. Never commit a generated `.docx`,
`.pptx`, `.xlsx`, `.pdf` or page image.

## 8. The limitation, stated in the report

This procedure **detects and fixes** layout defects; it does not **guarantee**
the document is right. The loop sees a LibreOffice render on this machine: it
does not see pagination as Word will compute it, font substitution on the
customer's machine, a mail-merge field that Word will fill from a data source, or
a CJK line break that differs between engines. Say that in the report, name what
was checked and how, and let a person open the file before it goes out.

# Producing a customer document: template, fill, look at it

Intro: two legs, one loop.

10	that puts the run's data into a template, and a **visual loop** that renders the
11	result and reads every page of it. A run that fills and does not look has not
12	finished the job; it has produced a file and does not know what is in it.

88	Substituting text is trivial; making the *conversion* keep the document's

90	found by rendering a draft that looked fine in the XML:
91	
92	- **State the East Asian font, size and language on every text style.** Without
93	  `style:font-name-asian` the exported docx carries
94	  `w:eastAsia="Noto Serif CJK SC"` — LibreOffice's default Asian face, a
95	  Simplified-Chinese serif — instead of the Noto Sans JP the template asked for;
96	  without `style:language-asian="ja"` it carries `w:lang w:eastAsia="en-US"`, so
97	  the reader treats Japanese as English for line breaking and fallback. The
98	  second defect is invisible in a render and only shows in the XML, which is the
99	  argument for checking both.
100	- **docx:** a heading needs `fo:keep-with-next="always"` (otherwise it strands at
101	  the foot of a page) and a table needs `style:may-break-between-rows="false"`.
102	- **pptx:** the page is 28 × 15.75 cm — LibreOffice's own 16:9 — and a
103	  `style:page-layout` naming any other 16:9 size is ignored, which misplaces every
104	  frame laid out for it. Text styles must be `style:family="paragraph"` with names
105	  no built-in Impress style uses (`Title` resolves to the built-in `Title` and the
106	  styling is lost). Paragraph spacing inside a slide's text box does not survive
107	  the export; use `fo:line-height`.
108	- **Keep the filled flat file.** `fill` writes `<out>.fodt`/`.fodp`/`.fods` beside
109	  the output for exactly this reason: the next fix is an edit there.

the document is right. The loop sees a LibreOffice render on this machine: it

Issue #420: フェーズ 2 — 顧客提出品質の設計書生成: スキル docs/customer-doc + スクリプト + 既定 flat ODF テンプレート + 3 形式通し実験

# フェーズ 2 — 顧客提出品質の設計書生成: スキル + スクリプト + 既定テンプレート + 通し実験

#232 フェーズ 2。フェーズ 1 の実測（#232 のコメント参照）で確定した配分の上に、顧客提出品質の pptx / docx / xlsx をエージェントが LibreOffice で作れるようにする。**スキル・スクリプト・既定テンプレート・通し実験を 1 つの単位**として実装する（#12 スレッドでの人による確定事項・2026-10-XX の指示）。フェーズ 1 の検証は完了済みで、配分は次の通り確定している:

- **flat ODF（.fodt/.fodp/.fods）のテキスト直書き** — ゼロから組む土台と、その**修正**（テキスト編集＋再変換で足りる）
- **UNO** — 利用者が渡すバイナリ様式を開いての**充填と修正**

## スコープ（成果物 4 点 + 判定 1 点）

1. **スキル `docs/customer-doc`** — design-doc（`src/content/skills/docs/design-doc.md`、runtime 側 `.github/atomaton/skills/docs/` にも同内容の実ファイルあり — 両者同期の文書化は無いので design-doc の前例通り**両方に置く**）と同じ形式で書く。含めるもの:
   - テンプレートの契約: 利用者が渡す様式パス or atomaton 既定テンプレート
   - 3 形式それぞれの充填手順 — **2 脚を書き分ける**: flat ODF 土台（テキスト編集＋`--convert-to`）／バイナリ様式（UNO: `program/python` で listener に接続）
   - 視覚検証ループの手順と予算: レンダ→画像 read→判定→修正→再レンダの閉ループ。**予算は枚数×画素数で書く** — 画像 1 枚のトークンコストは run の内側から観測できないためトークン数では書かない
   - vision の扱い: ループは vision: true の run（`engineer`/`reviewer`）か、vision 付き sub-run に押し込む。`atomaton`/`architect` は vision: false なのでループを自分の run で回さない、と明記
   - 報告の形（フェーズ 1 の表の形: 手順・コマンド・所要・成否）
   - 成果物の配布経路 — **この issue の中で決めてスキルに書く**。既知の事実: uploads endpoint は `ghs_` トークンで全面 404（#164 実測）で使えない。既存機構は orphan ブランチ（`attachments` サーバーの `publish_draft`、config の `tools.servers.attachments.settings.branch`、デフォルト `business-docs`、デフォルトブランチへの公開は拒否される）— これを基準に判断する
   - 品質の限定を明記: ループは「検出して直す」であって「保証する」ではない
2. **スクリプト** — `generate.mjs`（`src/content/skills/docs/generate.mjs:155` の 9 deb リスト）と同じ依存導入方式（tarball + `dpkg-deb -x`、root 不要・setup_commands に入れない）を再利用し、deb を **15 個**に増やす（+ `libobasis25.8-{calc,impress,pyuno}`）。実測: 213MB tarball 1.9s → 展開 3.7s → 582MB。
3. **既定テンプレート** — flat ODF テキスト（.fodt/.fodp/.fods）を `src/content/` 配下に置く（具体パスは design-doc の前例に合わせて判断）。プレースホルダ（`{{...}}`）を含み、テキスト差分が読めること。
4. **通し実験** — pptx / docx / xlsx それぞれ実物 1 通を、スキル+スクリプト+テンプレートでループ込み（レンダ→read→判定→修正→再レンダ）で作る。うち **1 通以上は利用者渡し風のバイナリ様式**で UNO 脚を実際に通す（フェーズ 1 の未検証箇所: コンテンツコントロール・差し込みフィールド・テーマ別フォントを持つ実物。`replaceAll` はプレーン文字列にしか効かない）。
5. **design-doc / generate.mjs の見直し判定** — この機能が入ったあと不要になる候補（design-doc スキルの「3 層を orphan ブランチに載せる」フロー、generate.mjs の単純変換部 = openpyxl/python-docx のゼロから生成）について **削除か縮小かの判定と根拠を PR に記録する**。依存導入機構と docx→PDF 変換は再利用するので残す。**判定の実行（削除・縮小の適用）はこの issue ではしない。**

## 実測済みの前提（調べ直さない）

<details>
<summary>フェーズ 1 の実測事実（Ubuntu 26.04 / root なし / LibreOffice 25.8.7.3）</summary>

- **導入**: tarball + `dpkg-deb -x` で 15 deb（`generate.mjs:155` の 9 + `libobasis25.8-{calc,impress,pyuno}`）で 3 形式＋UNO が動く。`program/python`（3.11.15）と `pyuno.so`・`uno.py` は `libobasis25.8-pyuno` 由来、Impress の `libsdlo.so` は `core`、Calc の `libsclo.so` は `calc` 由来。
- **UNO 実測**: `import uno` 0.045s / listener 接続 1.0s / 文書 1 通 0.1〜0.3s（docx・pptx・xlsx で文字置換・表行挿入・図形追加・セル書式変更→`storeToURL` 成立）。
- **UNO の罠**: 図形は `page.add(s)` の**後**に `s.setString()`（逆順だとテキストが保存されない）。相対パス不可（`uno.systemPathToFileUrl(os.path.abspath(p))`）。列挙値は `uno.Enum(...)`（`getConstantByName` は例外）。listener を kill すると `.~lock.<名前>#` が残り次の store が失敗 — `desktop.terminate()` で終わらせるかロックを消す。`--convert-to` は既存出力先を上書きするので再レンダで同じディレクトリ可。
- **flat ODF 実測**: 最小 XML をテキストで書き `--convert-to` で docx/pptx/xlsx へ 0.31〜1.41s。`{{PLACEHOLDER}}` は変換後も OOXML に残る。
- **レンダ**: `--convert-to png` は**1 文書 1 枚（1 ページ目）のみ**。全ページは `--convert-to pdf` → `pypdfium2`（`pip install pypdfium2 pillow` = 3.9s、150dpi 3 ページ 0.11s）。解像度指定は filter data JSON（例 `'png:impress_png_Export:{"PixelWidth":{"type":"long","value":1920},...}'`）。
- **CJK フォント必須**: 無いと全部豆腐でレイアウト判定不能。`apt-get download fonts-noto-cjk`（59MB, 2.0s）+ `dpkg-deb -x` + `~/.fonts` に .ttc 4 本（0.4s）。
- **画像の置き場所**: `files` サーバーの read が読めるのはリポジトリ内と `/tmp/atomaton-workspace` のみ。workspace は 5MB 上限 — レンダ画像は workspace 配下の小さなディレクトリに置く（リポジトリ内はコミットに混ざる）。
- **視覚ループ 1 周の実績**: レンダ 0.55s×2 + 修正 0.24s（+ listener 起動 ~2s）で欠陥 4 件検出・修正。**1 周で終わらない** — 2 周目に別欠陥（枠間の縦余白）が見えた。画像 1 枚 1654×931 で 15.7〜131KB。
</details>

## 制約

- `environment.setup_commands` は変更しない
- design-doc スキル自体の削除はしない（判定の記録のみ）
- リポジトリ原則: 生成物の定義（テンプレート・スクリプト）はテキストで差分が読めること。バイナリ成果物（.docx 等）そのものはリポジトリにコミットしない

## 検収基準（マージ済み PR で観測できること）

1. スキルファイルが存在し、スコープ 1 の 7 項目（契約／2 脚の手順／ループ+予算／vision の扱い／報告の形／配布経路の決定／品質の限定）をすべて含む
2. スクリプトで root 不要・秒単位に LibreOffice + UNO が導入でき、`environment.setup_commands` が変更されていない
3. 3 形式の既定テンプレートがテキストとして存在し、diff が読める
4. 3 形式それぞれ: ループ込みの実物 1 通の証跡（コマンド・所要・検出した欠陥と修正内容）が PR に載る。うち 1 通以上はバイナリ様式経由の UNO 脚
5. design-doc / generate.mjs の見直し判定が記録されている

## 閉じ条件

この issue の作業が載るブランチは **#232 のブランチ**（この子の PR は #232 のブランチへマージされる。デフォルトブランチには #12 がdeliverするまで何も載らない）。#232 のブランチ上のマージ済み PR ヘッドで検収基準 1〜5 が観測できたとき、この issue の担当 run が `request_close_issue` で閉じる。証跡は PR 本文とマージ済みヘッドのファイル。

## 依存と引き継ぎ

- 依存: なし（フェーズ 1 完了済み）
- フェーズ 1 のメモと再現スクリプト: `/tmp/atomaton-workspace/phase1/`（`NOTES.md` にコマンドと罠、`uno_fill.py` / `uno_defect.py` / `uno_fix.py` / `raster.py`、3 形式の最小 flat ODF、レンダ画像 2 枚）— 2026-11-03 時点で存在を確認済み
- 親のスレッド（#232 のフェーズ 1 コメント）に実測の詳細表がある。疑問が出たらまず親スレッドを読むこと

+# Producing a customer document: template, fill, then look at it
+
+A document that leaves the building is judged by how it looks, not by whether the
+file opened. So this procedure has two halves that cannot be separated: a **fill**
+that puts the run's data into a template, and a **visual loop** that renders the
+result and reads every page of it. A run that fills and does not look has not
+finished the job; it has produced a file and does not know what is in it.
+
+The scripts, both beside this file in the shipped tree:
+
+| Script | What it is for |
+| --- | --- |
+| `customer-doc.mjs` | `deps`, `template`, `fill`, `render`, `uno` — this procedure |
+| `deps.mjs` | the one dependency install both this and `docs/design-doc`'s `generate.mjs` use |
+
+Dependencies are installed on demand into the cache directory and never into
+`environment.setup_commands`. `bun customer-doc.mjs deps` installs and reports
+everything the other subcommands use, so a first run on a machine pays once:
+measured 9–39 s for LibreOffice (a 213 MB tarball, 15 `.deb`s extracted, 584 MB

+for the two pip packages. Every later run says `cached` for all of them and takes
+under a second.

+## 1. Which leg — decided by the template, not by preference
+
+| Template | Leg | What it means |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `.fodt` / `.fodp` / `.fods`, or the name `docx`/`pptx`/`xlsx` | **flat ODF** | the placeholders are substituted in XML text, then converted to the binary format by LibreOffice |
+| any other path — a customer's `.docx`, `.pptx`, `.xlsx` | **UNO** | a headless LibreOffice opens the template, replaces the placeholders in the document model, and stores it back |
+
+```bash
+bun customer-doc.mjs fill --template docx --data data.json --out out/report.docx
+bun customer-doc.mjs fill --template /path/to/customer-form.docx --data data.json --out out/form.docx
+bun customer-doc.mjs render out/report.docx --outdir out/render --dpi 120
+```
+
+Prefer the flat leg. Its source is text, so a fix is an edit in a diff and one
+more conversion — not a round trip through a binary that rewrites everything it
+touches. The UNO leg exists for the template you were handed, and for that one it
+is the only leg there is.

+## 2. The templates and the placeholder contract
+
+Three defaults ship under `templates/`, each a flat ODF file with a comment header
+that states what was measured about it:
+
+| File | Format | Shape |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `report.fodt` | docx | A4 portrait, title page, 概要 / システム構成 / スケジュール / 費用 / 体制・連絡先, footer with page numbers |
+| `deck.fodp` | pptx | 16:9, three slides: title, agenda, content-with-bullets |
+| `book.fods` | xlsx | two sheets: 見積 (itemised, formulas for 小計/消費税/合計) and 前提条件 |

+A placeholder is `{{UPPER_SNAKE}}` and is substituted everywhere it appears,
+including inside table cells. Values are XML-escaped, so a name with `&` or `<`
+in it is safe. The data file is one JSON object, one key per placeholder.
+
+Three properties of a *spreadsheet* template are not free choices, each measured
+by filling and re-rendering:
+

+  text. The value is what the format carries as a number and what a formula
+  reads; the text is what the cell displays. Text alone makes it a text cell —
+  no number format, no right alignment, and a formula pointing at it computes
+  nothing;

+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `keysNotInTemplate` | data keys no placeholder matched | the data or the template is wrong; do not ship |
+| `leftInTemplate` | placeholders still in the output | a typo in the key, or the placeholder is not plain text |
+| `unfilled` | keys the fill could not place | same as above, and the reason this field exists |

+#!/usr/bin/env bun
+/**
+ * customer-doc.mjs — fill a template and render the result, for the three Office
+ * formats a customer opens: docx, pptx, xlsx.
+ *
+ *     bun customer-doc.mjs deps
+ *     bun customer-doc.mjs template docx [--out DIR]
+ *     bun customer-doc.mjs fill --template <path|docx|pptx|xlsx> --data <json> --out <path>
+ *     bun customer-doc.mjs render <file> --outdir DIR [--dpi 150] [--pages 1-3]
+ *     bun customer-doc.mjs uno --script <file.py> [--args ...]
+ *
+ * Two legs, and which one runs is decided by the template:
+ *
+ * - a `.fodt`/`.fodp`/`.fods` template (the shipped ones under `templates/`, or
+ *   the agent's copy of one) is filled **as text** — placeholders substituted in
+ *   the XML, then `--convert-to` the requested binary format. The filled flat
+ *   file is kept next to the output because it is the diffable source: a fix is
+ *   an edit there and one more conversion, not a round trip through a binary.
+ * - any other template (a customer's `.docx`, `.pptx`, `.xlsx` — the ones with a
+ *   theme, content controls and mail-merge fields) is filled **over UNO**: a
+ *   headless LibreOffice is started, the template opened, the placeholders
+ *   replaced, and the result stored in the same format.
+ *
+ * Every subcommand ends with one JSON line on stdout and progress on stderr, the
+ * shape `docs/design-doc`'s `generate.mjs` uses so a run reads both the same way.
+ */
+import { spawn, spawnSync } from "node:child_process";
+import {
+  copyFileSync,
+  existsSync,
+  mkdirSync,
+  mkdtempSync,
+  readFileSync,
+  readdirSync,
+  rmSync,
+  statSync,
+  writeFileSync,
+} from "node:fs";
+import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
+import { basename, dirname, join, resolve } from "node:path";
+import { CACHE_DIR, convert, deps, ensure, record } from "./deps.mjs";
+
+const HERE = dirname(new URL(import.meta.url).pathname);
+const TEMPLATES = join(HERE, "templates");
+
+/** The shipped default template per output format, as flat ODF text. */
+const DEFAULT_TEMPLATES = {
+  docx: "report.fodt",
+  pptx: "deck.fodp",
+  xlsx: "book.fods",
+};
+
+/** The filter LibreOffice needs to write each format; the extension alone is not enough for UNO. */
+const FILTERS = {
+  docx: "MS Word 2007 XML",
+  pptx: "Impress MS PowerPoint 2007 XML",
+  xlsx: "Calc MS Excel 2007 XML",
+  pdf: "writer_pdf_Export",
+  odt: "writer8",
+  otf: "writer8",
+  odp: "impress8",
+  ods: "calc8",
+};
+
+const argv = process.argv.slice(2);
+const command = argv[0];
+const rest = argv.slice(1);
+
+function flag(name) {
+  const i = rest.indexOf(name);
+  return i >= 0 ? rest[i + 1] : undefined;
+}
+
+function fail(message) {
+  console.error(`customer-doc: ${message}`);
+  process.exit(1);
+}
+
+/** The one line a caller reads: one JSON object, no indent, so the last line of stdout is the summary. */
+function emit(result) {
+  console.log(JSON.stringify({ ...result, deps }));
+}
+
+const extensionOf = (path) => (/\.[^.\\/]+$/.exec(path)?.[0] ?? "").slice(1).toLowerCase();
+
+// ------------------------------------------------------------------- deps
+
+/** Install and report everything the other subcommands use, so a run can time it once. */
+function commandDeps() {
+  const { soffice, python, unoPython } = ensure({
+    lo: true,
+    cjk: true,
+    packages: [
+      { pip: "pypdfium2", module: "pypdfium2" },
+      { pip: "pillow", module: "PIL" },
+    ],
+    uno: true,
+  });
+  emit({ soffice, python, unoPython });
+}
+
+// ------------------------------------------------------------------- template
+
+/**
+ * The default template for a format, as a path; with `--out`, a copy of it.
+ *
+ * The copy is the point of the leg the skill calls "fix it in the text": the
+ * shipped file is read-only in spirit (it is the template every run starts from),
+ * and an edit belongs in the run's own copy, converted again to see the result.
+ */
+function commandTemplate() {
+  const format = rest[0];
+  const name = DEFAULT_TEMPLATES[format];
+  if (!name) fail(`usage: customer-doc.mjs template <${Object.keys(DEFAULT_TEMPLATES).join("|")}> [--out DIR]`);
+  const source = join(TEMPLATES, name);
+  if (!existsSync(source)) fail(`default template missing: ${source}`);
+  const outdir = flag("--out");
+  if (!outdir) {
+    emit({ format, template: source });
+    return;
+  }
+  mkdirSync(outdir, { recursive: true });
+  const target = join(outdir, name);
+  copyFileSync(source, target);
+  emit({ format, template: target });
+}
+
+// ------------------------------------------------------------------- fill
+
+/** The template path `fill` was given: a shipped format name, or a file. */
+function templatePath(value) {
+  if (!value) fail("fill: --template <path|docx|pptx|xlsx> is required");
+  const name = DEFAULT_TEMPLATES[value];
+  if (!name) return resolve(value);
+  const shipped = join(TEMPLATES, name);
+  if (!existsSync(shipped)) fail(`default template missing: ${shipped}`);
+  return shipped;
+}
+
+function readData(path) {
+  if (!path) fail("fill: --data <json> is required");
+  let raw;
+  try {
+    raw = readFileSync(resolve(path), "utf8");
+  } catch {
+    fail(`fill: cannot read --data ${path}`);
+  }
+  let data;
+  try {
+    data = JSON.parse(raw);
+  } catch (e) {
+    fail(`fill: --data ${path} is not JSON: ${e.message}`);
+  }
+  if (typeof data !== "object" || data === null || Array.isArray(data)) fail("fill: --data must be a JSON object");
+  // `{{KEY}}` is the placeholder a flat ODF template can hold without any
+  // machinery, and the key is what goes inside it; a nested value has no spelling
+  // there, so it is refused here rather than silently becoming "[object Object]".
+  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(data)) {
+    if (typeof value === "object" && value !== null) fail(`fill: --data.${key} must be a string or a number`);
+  }
+  return data;
+}
+
+const xmlEscape = (text) => String(text).replaceAll("&", "&").replaceAll("<", "<").replaceAll(">", ">");
+
+const PLACEHOLDER = /\{\{[A-Z0-9_]+\}\}/g;
+
+/**
+ * The flat ODF leg: substitute in the XML, then convert.
+ *
+ * The filled flat file stays in the output directory. It is the version a diff
+ * shows and the one a fix edits — the binary is a rendering of it, not the thing
+ * to edit — so deleting it would leave the next round with nothing readable.
+ */
+function fillFlat({ template, data, out }) {
+  const t0 = Date.now();
+  // The flat file lands beside the output, and the caller's `--out` names a
+  // directory that need not exist yet: the skill's own first example is
+  // `--out out/report.docx` on a tree with no `out/`, and the UNO leg already
+  // creates it (`fillUno`). Without this the write below throws ENOENT before any
+  // conversion has happened, which reads as a broken script rather than a missing
+  // directory.
+  mkdirSync(dirname(resolve(out)), { recursive: true });

Defect 5 confirmed: `libreOffice()` returns `"soffice"` (PATH binary) on line ~89 without checking `program/python`. Then `unoPython()` at customer-doc.mjs:313 requires `CACHE_DIR/lo-root/.../program/python`.

Fix approach: the PATH office has its own `program/python` somewhere — but resolving it robustly is awkward. Options:
(a) When a UNO interpreter is needed, ensure() must guarantee the cached one. Add an option to `ensure({uno: true})` / `libreOffice({uno: true})` that skips the PATH short-circuit when the cached python is absent, i.e. installs the tarball anyway.
(b) Resolve the PATH office's `program/python`.

Which is cleaner? The PATH branch exists to avoid a download when LibreOffice is already installed. For the UNO leg we need `import uno` in *an* interpreter that matches the PATH office. Deriving the PATH soffice's program dir: `readlink -f $(command -v soffice)` → `<program>/soffice`; then `<program>/python`. That's a fair amount of machinery and may still fail (distro's python may lack uno).

Simplest, most predictable: `libreOffice({ uno })` — when `uno: true`, require the *cached* install (soffice + program/python) because UNO's interpreter ships with the tarball; only short-circuit to PATH when `uno` is false. And with `uno: true` and a PATH soffice present, we still install the tarball into the cache — 39s once, but correct and the cached path is what `unoPython()` uses. Hmm, that means a machine with LibreOffice installed downloads 213MB when filling a binary template. Acceptable? It's the honest trade: the tarball's `program/python` is the interpreter whose `uno` module is guaranteed to match.

Alternative: try the PATH office's `program/python` first if it exists and can `import uno`. That gives the fast path on distro installs, and falls back to the tarball. Implementation: in `libreOffice({uno})`, when a PATH soffice exists:
- if !uno → return "soffice"
- read the real path of soffice (spawnSync("readlink", ["-f", resolvedPath])), take dirname, check `<dir>/python` exists and `spawnSync(<dir>/python, ["-c","import uno"]).status === 0` → return "soffice" and *record the interpreter* for `unoPython()`.
That requires `unoPython()` to know the chosen interpreter. So `ensure` should return `{soffice, python, ...}` — `python` currently is the venv python (for pypdfium2/docx). In customer-doc.mjs, `unoPython()` uses CACHE_DIR path directly.

Cleaner design: `ensure()` returns an extra key `unoPython` — the interpreter that can `import uno`, resolved by: if the cached LO has program/python → that; else if PATH soffice → probe its sibling `python`; else undefined. And `libreOffice({uno:true})` ensures at least one is available (installing tarball when neither works).

Part of #420
Phase 2 of #232 — the customer-document skill, its script, three flat ODF templates, and the experiment that measured them.

A customer document is judged by how it looks, so the skill is a fill **and** a look. The scripts and the templates are the delivery; the measurements below are what the templates' comment headers and the skill's rules are built on.

## What is in here

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `skills/docs/customer-doc.md` | the skill: two legs, the visual loop, budget, vision split, report shape, distribution, limitation |
| `skills/docs/customer-doc.mjs` | `deps`, `template`, `fill`, `render`, `uno`; one JSON line per call |
| `skills/docs/deps.mjs` | the LibreOffice + CJK + venv install, shared with `generate.mjs` |
| `skills/docs/templates/{report.fodt,deck.fodp,book.fods}` | flat ODF templates for docx / pptx / xlsx |

Templates are flat ODF text on purpose: a fix is an edit in a diff and one more conversion, so they are reviewable and text-diffable. No generated binary, PDF or page image is committed.

## The experiment: three formats, both legs

**Flat leg** — `fill --template docx|pptx|xlsx` then `render`, with the visual loop run on every page:

| Format | Pages | Fill | Render | Defects found by looking, and the rule that fixed each |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| docx (`report.fodt`) | 3 | 0.30 s | 0.6 s | serif CJK instead of sans, and a heading stranded at the foot of a page → `style:font-name-asian` + `style:language-asian="ja"`, `fo:keep-with-next="always"` |
| pptx (`deck.fodp`) | 3 | 0.27 s | 0.6 s | every frame misplaced → the page must be LibreOffice's own 16:9 (28 × 15.75 cm); text at Impress defaults → paragraph styles must be `style:family="paragraph"` with non-builtin names; bullet spacing lost → `fo:line-height` |
| xlsx (`book.fods`) | 2 | 0.27 s | 0.7 s | all totals 0 円 → a formula cell must not carry a cached `office:value`; 4 print pages instead of 2 → `style:page-layout` must sit in `office:automatic-styles`; `###` in 合計 → column width |

After the fixes: 見積 with 3 items, 小計 46,000,000 / 消費税 4,600,000 / 合計（税込）50,600,000 円, one page per sheet, header and footer on both.

**UNO leg** — a "customer-supplied" binary docx built to hold a placeholder four ways (plain run, run split in two, content control, `MERGEFIELD` result, plus a table cell): **5 of 6 keys filled**. The split run and the content control both worked, because the search runs over the text model; the one inside the mail-merge field came back as `unfilled`, because a field's result is not in the searchable text. `w:sdt` and `w:instrText MERGEFIELD` both survived the store, so the fix is to move that placeholder, not to abandon the template — and the render of the output shows `{{AUTHOR}}` still there, which is what makes `unfilled` trustworthy.

**One attribute check a render cannot do.** With `style:font-name-asian` removed the export writes `w:eastAsia="Noto Serif CJK SC"`; with `style:language-asian="ja"` removed it writes `w:lang w:eastAsia="en-US"`. The second is invisible in a picture, so the skill states the loop as two checks: read the pages, then confirm in the file what a page cannot show.

## The judgement asked for, recorded and **not applied**

**`generate.mjs`'s zero-from-scratch builders: shrink, do not delete.**
The two scripts answer different inputs — `generate.mjs` builds a document from a Markdown draft that has no template, `customer-doc.mjs` fills a template a person authored — so merging them would make the draft path depend on a template that does not exist. What *was* duplicated and is now gone is the install and the docx→PDF spawn: both live in `deps.mjs` and `generate.mjs` imports them (−170 lines). **Applied, and verified behaviour-preserving**: the same draft through the pre-refactor script (from `HEAD`) and through this one produced a byte-identical `design.docx` (36,929 B) and `design.pdf` (48,625 B); `design.xlsx` differs by one byte of metadata. A second run reports every dependency `cached`. Deleting the builders themselves was **not** applied.

**`docs/design-doc`'s orphan-branch flow: keep, shrink the narration, do not replace.**
It is the only route left for binaries here — the upload endpoint refuses a `ghs_` Actions token — and it does not touch the run's worktree, which is exactly what a customer delivery needs. §7 of the new skill points at that measurement instead of restating it. No change was made to `design-doc.md` or to its publish calls.

`bun run typecheck` clean; `bun run test` 2174 pass, 0 fail. `scan_secrets` could not resolve gitleaks in this environment (`::warning::`, so the branch was not scanned for credentials); nothing added here reads a credential.

Part of #420
Phase 2 of #232 — the customer-document skill, its script, three flat ODF templates, and the experiment that measured them.

A customer document is judged by how it looks, so the skill is a fill **and** a look. The scripts and the templates are the delivery; the measurements below are what the templates' comment headers and the skill's rules are built on.

## What is in here

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `skills/docs/customer-doc.md` | the skill: two legs, the visual loop, budget, vision split, report shape, distribution, limitation |
| `skills/docs/customer-doc.mjs` | `deps`, `template`, `fill`, `render`, `uno`; one JSON line per call |
| `skills/docs/deps.mjs` | the LibreOffice + CJK + venv install, shared with `generate.mjs` |
| `skills/docs/templates/{report.fodt,deck.fodp,book.fods}` | flat ODF templates for docx / pptx / xlsx |

Templates are flat ODF text on purpose: a fix is an edit in a diff and one more conversion, so they are reviewable and text-diffable. No generated binary, PDF or page image is committed.

## The experiment: three formats, both legs

**Flat leg** — `fill --template docx|pptx|xlsx` then `render`, with the visual loop run on every page:

| Format | Pages | Fill | Render | Defects found by looking, and the rule that fixed each |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| docx (`report.fodt`) | 3 | 0.30 s | 0.6 s | serif CJK instead of sans, and a heading stranded at the foot of a page → `style:font-name-asian` + `style:language-asian="ja"`, `fo:keep-with-next="always"` |
| pptx (`deck.fodp`) | 3 | 0.27 s | 0.6 s | every frame misplaced → the page must be LibreOffice's own 16:9 (28 × 15.75 cm); text at Impress defaults → paragraph styles must be `style:family="paragraph"` with non-builtin names; bullet spacing lost → `fo:line-height` |
| xlsx (`book.fods`) | 2 | 0.27 s | 0.7 s | all totals 0 円 → a formula cell must not carry a cached `office:value`; 4 print pages instead of 2 → `style:page-layout` must sit in `office:automatic-styles`; `###` in 合計 → column width |

After the fixes: 見積 with 3 items, 小計 46,000,000 / 消費税 4,600,000 / 合計（税込）50,600,000 円, one page per sheet, header and footer on both.

**UNO leg** — a "customer-supplied" binary docx built to hold a placeholder four ways (plain run, run split in two, content control, `MERGEFIELD` result, plus a table cell): **5 of 6 keys filled**. The split run and the content control both worked, because the search runs over the text model; the one inside the mail-merge field came back as `unfilled`, because a field's result is not in the searchable text. `w:sdt` and `w:instrText MERGEFIELD` both survived the store, so the fix is to move that placeholder, not to abandon the template — and the render of the output shows `{{AUTHOR}}` still there, which is what makes `unfilled` trustworthy.

**One attribute check a render cannot do.** With `style:font-name-asian` removed the export writes `w:eastAsia="Noto Serif CJK SC"`; with `style:language-asian="ja"` removed it writes `w:lang w:eastAsia="en-US"`. The second is invisible in a picture, so the skill states the loop as two checks: read the pages, then confirm in the file what a page cannot show.

## The judgement asked for, recorded and **not applied**

**`generate.mjs`'s zero-from-scratch builders: shrink, do not delete.**
The two scripts answer different inputs — `generate.mjs` builds a document from a Markdown draft that has no template, `customer-doc.mjs` fills a template a person authored — so merging them would make the draft path depend on a template that does not exist. What *was* duplicated and is now gone is the install and the docx→PDF spawn: both live in `deps.mjs` and `generate.mjs` imports them (−170 lines). **Applied, and verified behaviour-preserving**: the same draft through the pre-refactor script (from `HEAD`) and through this one produced a byte-identical `design.docx` (36,929 B) and `design.pdf` (48,625 B); `design.xlsx` differs by one byte of metadata. A second run reports every dependency `cached`. Deleting the builders themselves was **not** applied.

**`docs/design-doc`'s orphan-branch flow: keep, shrink the narration, do not replace.**
It is the only route left for binaries here — the upload endpoint refuses a `ghs_` Actions token — and it does not touch the run's worktree, which is exactly what a customer delivery needs. §7 of the new skill points at that measurement instead of restating it. No change was made to `design-doc.md` or to its publish calls.

## Checks

`bun run typecheck` clean; `bun run test` 2174 pass, 0 fail. `scan_secrets` could not resolve gitleaks in this environment (`::warning::`, so the branch was not scanned for credentials); nothing added here reads a credential.

## What a person should look at

1. `book.fods` page 1 — the totals are formulas, so a reader opening it in Excel should see 50,600,000 rather than a stale cached value.
2. `deck.fodp` — the title slide is a navy hero, slides 2–3 are white with a footer. Deliberate, but a style call a reviewer may want to change.
3. The skill's §5 vision split — `atomaton`/`architect` have no vision, so they must hand the image reading to an agent that does.
